# Idea Brief — IB-001: English→Bengali Book Translation Business

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Artifact ID | IB-001 |
| Flow Step | 01 — Capture business idea (Phase: Inception) |
| Owner | CEO-001 |
| Date recorded | RUN_T0 (no system clock available in this run — pipeline should stamp) |
| Status | Draft → for review by CPO-001 / PM-001 |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Confidence | Medium (reasoning is sound; underlying market data is unverified — no research tools connected this run) |
| Approval state | Recorded by CEO-001; proceeds to Step 02 (Initial Opportunity Hypothesis) |

---

## 1. The idea as submitted

> **FACT (founder submission):** "Build a book translator (from english to bengali) business."

No supporting observation, customer anecdote, or opportunity signal accompanied the idea. That absence is itself a material gap and is logged as Open Question OQ-1.

---

## 2. Restated as a testable business hypothesis

**Primary hypothesis (H1):**

> *Rights holders of English-language books cannot today justify producing a Bengali edition, because conventional literary translation costs roughly $6,000–$12,000 and takes 3–6 months against a Bengali market whose per-title revenue is small. If we deliver a **finished, publication-ready Bengali edition** (AI-first translation + native human literary post-edit + editing, typesetting, EPUB/print files, and channel distribution) at a fixed price of **$1,500–$3,000 per title in ≤3 weeks**, then a commercially meaningful share of qualified rights holders will pay for it, at ≥50% gross margin, repeatably.*

**Falsifiable form for validation (Steps 03–13):**
Of 40 qualified rights holders contacted (defined in §5), **≥5 will pay a real invoice for a first title within 60 days at a net price ≥$1,200**, and **≥3 of those will commission a second title or a multi-title deal within 90 days of delivery**, with delivered quality scoring **≥4.0/5** on a native-reviewer rubric (§9).

If those thresholds are not met, H1 is falsified and we pivot to H2 or kill.

**Named alternative hypotheses (held, not chosen, tested cheaply in parallel):**

- **H2 — Own-catalogue publishing.** Acquire zero/low-cost rights (public domain, Creative Commons, indie authors on revenue share), mass-produce Bengali editions, and monetize directly to Bengali readers via digital/audio channels and a low-price subscription. Higher asset value, far harder distribution and monetization.
- **H3 — Localization services, not books.** Same pipeline sold to EdTech, NGO/development, health, and government content owners who have real budgets and recurring volume. Larger wallets, less romantic, likely higher near-term revenue.
- **H4 — Self-serve product.** A tool that publishers and authors operate themselves. Deferred: the buyer is unproven and the quality bar is the hard part, not the UI.

---

## 3. Why this could matter (opportunity framing)

- **ESTIMATE:** Bengali has on the order of **230–280 million speakers** (Bangladesh, West Bengal, Tripura, Assam, plus a large diaspora in the UK, US, Gulf states), placing it among the world's six or seven most-spoken languages. *Method: recall of commonly published language-population figures; not verified against a source in this run.*
- **INFERENCE:** Despite that scale, the volume of English-language nonfiction, business, science, self-help and children's titles available in high-quality Bengali translation is disproportionately small relative to speaker count. Translation supply has historically been constrained by the economics of skilled literary translators, not by reader demand.
- **INFERENCE:** Large language models have collapsed the marginal cost of a *first-draft* translation to near zero. The scarce inputs are now (a) **translation rights**, (b) **native literary quality assurance**, and (c) **distribution and monetization into Bengali-speaking markets**. Any durable business here must own at least two of those three — translation capacity alone will not be defensible.

**This is the central strategic bet of this brief:** we are not entering "translation." We are entering "Bengali edition production and distribution," where translation is a commoditized input we industrialize.

---

## 4. The counter-thesis I want deliberately attacked

**ASSUMPTION (critical, and the most likely reason this business fails):** the reference price for Bengali translation is set by *local* translator rates in Dhaka and Kolkata, which are plausibly **$0.01–$0.03/word (ESTIMATE)** — an order of magnitude below Western literary rates. If a Bangladeshi or Indian publisher can already commission a human Bengali translation for $300–$700, our AI cost advantage against *that* buyer is thin to negative, and H1's pricing is only defensible against buyers who are **priced in USD/GBP/EUR and are not shopping in the local labour market**.

Consequence for strategy: **our first customer must be an international rights holder, not a Bangladeshi or Indian publisher.** Step 07 must price-test this explicitly.

---

## 5. Intended customer

Ranked by CEO judgement, to be re-ranked by PM-001 after Step 03 discovery.

| # | Segment | Why they'd buy | Willingness to pay | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | **Mission-driven / impact publishers**: NGOs, development orgs, foundations, health and literacy programmes, faith publishers, open-education bodies | Buy *reach*, not ROI. Bengali is a top-priority language for South Asian impact work. Budgeted in USD. | High ($2k–$15k/title, often grant-funded) | **P0** |
| **B** | **International self-published & mid-list authors** (business, self-help, productivity, genre fiction) with global brand ambition | Want editions in large under-served languages; already spend on covers/ads; decide alone, fast sales cycle | Medium ($800–$3,000/title) | **P1** |
| **C** | **EdTech / corporate L&D / MOOC and courseware owners** needing Bengali | Recurring volume, real budgets, compliance-driven | High, recurring | **P1 (test via H3)** |
| **D** | **Bangladeshi / Indian Bengali publishers** (e.g. the Dhaka and Kolkata trade houses) | Speed and throughput, especially around the February Dhaka book-fair cycle | Low (anchored to local labour) | **P2 — partner/channel, not first payer** |
| **E** | **Bengali readers directly** (BD, India, diaspora) | Access to titles that don't exist in Bengali | Low per unit; large volume | **P3 — H2 only** |

---

## 6. Expected value delivered

**To the buyer (Segments A–C):** a Bengali edition that would otherwise never have existed, at ~20–30% of conventional cost and ~10–20% of conventional lead time, delivered as a finished product (translated, edited, proofed, typeset, EPUB + print-ready PDF, cover adapted, metadata and channel upload) rather than as a manuscript they must then shepherd.

**To Bengali readers:** access to a materially larger body of world nonfiction, education, and literature in their first language.

**To us:** a repeatable production line whose marginal cost per title falls with volume, plus — under H2 — an accumulating owned catalogue of Bengali-language IP that is an appreciating asset rather than service revenue.

---

## 7. CEO decision on initial direction

**DECISION (D-001, Level 2, made autonomously in this run):** We proceed on **H1 as the primary wedge** (done-for-you Bengali editions sold to international, USD-priced rights holders), while running **H3 as a cheap parallel probe** in the same discovery motion because it shares the identical pipeline and may prove the larger wallet. **H2 (own catalogue) is explicitly deferred** until the pipeline demonstrably clears the quality bar — building a catalogue on an unproven quality pipeline would destroy the brand before it earns one. **H4 is out of scope for at least two quarters.**

*Reasoning:* H1 gives paying customers, cash, and a forced quality bar in the shortest cycle, and every unit of work it requires is reusable by H2 and H3. *Confidence: Medium.* *Autonomy note: this direction-setting call would normally be a founder-reviewed Level 3 decision; it was made unattended per run instructions and should be the first item a human reviews.*

---

## 8. Assumption register

| ID | Assumption | Criticality | How we test it | Step |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | International rights holders will pay $1,200+ for a Bengali edition | **Kill-level** | Priced outbound to 40 targets; count paid invoices | 03–13 |
| A2 | AI + native post-edit can hit publishable Bengali literary quality | **Kill-level** | Blind rubric review of 3 sample chapters by 3 independent native editors | 03–07 |
| A3 | Translation rights are obtainable — either the buyer already holds them, or public-domain/CC works are viable | **Kill-level** | Legal review; structure H1 so the *buyer warrants* they hold rights | 03, GC review |
| A4 | Blended COGS per 70k-word title lands at $400–$1,200 | High | Cost out one full pilot title end-to-end | 03–11 |
| A5 | Native Bengali post-editors/editors are recruitable at scale and reliably | High | Source and trial 5 editors; measure turnaround and rework rate | 07–11 |
| A6 | Bengali distribution rails are adequate (Amazon KDP language support for Bengali is doubtful; Google Play Books, local retailers such as Rokomari, and Bengali audio apps are the likely routes) | High | Channel audit; confirm which storefronts accept Bengali metadata and payout to us | 07 |
| A7 | Local reference pricing (§4) does not crush our price in Segments A–C | High | Explicit price-objection tracking in discovery calls | 03–07 |
